newsitem.title: FRANCE: France throws jobs dilemma back at carmakers.
newsitem.headline: France throws jobs dilemma back at carmakers.

text.p: The French government's refusal to foot the bill for restructuring the car industry highlights the dilemma of companies struggling to become more competitive at a time when job cuts are politically taboo.

The Industry Ministry said on Wednesday it had turned down a request from carmakers Renault SA and PSA Peugeot Citroen to pay the bulk of the cost of a massive early retirement programme at the two companies.

The companies say they need to cut the age and size of their workforces, among the oldest in the European car industry, to survive competition expected to grow even fiercer when the market opens up to the Japanese in the year 2000.
"Overmanning at both these companies is likely to become a problem," said analyst Keith Hayes at Goldman Sachs. "It will get to the point where they'll have no choice."
Renault, which has forecast a big loss for 1996, announced on Thursday afternoon that it would close Renault Industrie Belgique, an assembly plant in Belgium that employs 3,100 people.
It said the closure was "part of a major effort to streamline its industrial facilities" in a statement that hinted at further restructuring moves even closer to home.
Although the car industry is widely known to be in trouble, the French government's response came as no surprise after it turned down a similar request from the construction industry.
"In the current context, it's understandable that the government should say no," said a spokeswoman for the PSA group, which makes Peugeot and Citroen vehicles.

French unemployment is at a postwar high of 12.7 percent, and the government is trying to stave off pressure to reduce the retirement age and struggling to hold down public spending to comply with the criteria for European monetary union.

"There's a lot of pressure brought to bear on companies to keep them from cutting jobs, but companies are saying it's a big, bad world out there and they need to restructure to remain competitive," a car analyst said.

Peugeot and Renault had proposed 40,000 early retirements over six years out of a combined work force of 260,000 in exchange for taking on 14,000 young workers. The cost to the government was estimated at more than 35 billion francs.

"It's understandable that the government won't volunteer to subsidize the restructuring of the industry. European governments aren't overwhelmed with spare cash at the moment," said analyst Nick Snee at J.P. Morgan.

Analysts say the government also fears setting a precedent. French banks, insurance companies and airlines are waiting behind the car and construction industries to shed workers and bring costs into line with those of their international rivals.
But the car industry has been the most forthright in challenging the taboo on axing jobs.
Peugeot chairman Jacques Calvet said in December that if the government did not support the early retirement proposal, the company may have to lay off workers.

Tyremaker Michelin last week said it planned to cut 1,445 jobs in France in a drive to increase productivity but hoped to avoid layoffs. Components maker Valeo said last week it planned to regroup its European production plants.

"This restructuring won't translate overall into job cuts," Valeo chairman Noel Goutard told the magazine L'Expansion. "But on the other hand, companies aren't created to remain inert, nor to be the battleground of the class war."
The issue is most critical for French car makers. Their home market is crumbling after the expiry of more than two years of state-subsidized incentives. January sales fell 34 percent.
In the slow-growing European market, PSA and Renault ranked fifth and sixth among the big six European carmakers in January.
"The problem of the French industry is the lack of scale -- Volkswagen produces four million units, Peugeot and Renault produce around half that many," Snee said.
